position.answer: George was a Glasgow legal professional, lender and charitable founder. His family links retain their existing assessment; his exact birth and day of death remain qualified by conflicting published accounts.
points: Birth 1550–1560 is a published range, not an exact birthday.
Published descriptions support George’s marriage to Elspeth Craig. Janet’s mother and possible identity with the unnamed 1588 girl remain unresolved.

biography_sections.title: Legal career, property and philanthropy
biography_sections.markdown:
George Hutcheson of Lambhill was a Glasgow notary, public writer, lender and landowner whose professional business included work for the city, the University and ecclesiastical patrons. His interests combined legal practice, lending on bonds and an extensive property portfolio. The modern Oxford Dictionary of National Biography places his birth between 1550 and 1560, rather than supplying an exact birthday or proved birthplace. His father Thomas Hutcheson remains assessed as confident; no new confidence grade is proposed.

Sources: [ODNB public extract](https://doi.org/10.1093/ref:odnb/14275) and [History of GlasgowII,chXX](https://www.electricscotland.com/history/glasgow/glasgow2_20.htm).

biography_sections.title: Hospital and school: separate stages
biography_sections.markdown: George's deed of 16 December 1639 endowed a charitable hospital for poor older men with Trongate property and 20,000 merks. Thomas ratified the foundation in 1640 and added adjoining property and 20,200 merks for the lodging and education of twelve poor boys by his deed of 9 March 1641. Hospital here means charitable maintenance and accommodation, not a modern medical hospital. The foundation stone on 19 March 1641 and the first recorded boy's admission on 13 November 1643 are separate stages. Hill's published account says Archibald Edmiston initially attended the existing town schools; it does not show that the new foundation already taught all pupils on its own premises. Later incorporation in 1821 was not the original foundation. Sources: [Hill (1881), pp.58–63 and Appendix pp.239–252](https://archive.org/details/historyofhospita00hutc/page/58/mode/2up), [pp.203–204](https://archive.org/details/historyofhospita00hutc/page/203/mode/2up), and [the school's institutional history](https://www.hutchesons.org/our-school/our-history/). Hill's searchable published text was reviewed; manuscript deeds and admission minutes were not inspected. Conflicting published endowment totals are not silently harmonised; amounts are historical merks, with no modern purchasing-power conversion.

biography_sections.title: Published death-date evidence
biography_sections.markdown: Hill’s institutional history (1881), printed p.37, has now been visually checked. It reports 26 December 1639 and burial on the east side of the Cathedral, footnoting George’s Testament Testamentar. This makes 26 December the better-attributed published claim in the sources reviewed here. Henderson’s DNB (1891) gives 31 December and south-side burial without a date-specific citation. The cited testament remains uninspected, so the discrepancy is unresolved at the original-record level. [Hill, p.37](https://archive.org/details/historyofhospita00hutc/page/37/mode/1up).

biography_sections.title: Marriage, children and succession
biography_sections.markdown:
Hill reproduces the 28 August 1588 kirk-session entry, which records an unnamed girl born to George and Elizabeth (Elspeth) Craig and orders their marriage within a month. Hill also describes later infeftments granting Elspeth a liferent and discusses her 1632 testament and codicil as the records of George’s wife. These later records support the marriage. The kirk-session order supplies no date for the wedding.

The 1679 burgh order names Janet Hutcheson in Holland as George’s natural daughter. Hill inferred that she was a different person from the unnamed girl in the 1588 entry. The evidence reviewed leaves that identity and Janet’s mother unresolved. George’s published will names his brother Thomas as executor, and Hill reports Thomas’s service as George’s heir in 1640. Those roles do not establish how many children George had. The underlying records remain uninspected. [Hill (1881), printed pp. 35–38 and p. 47 n. 2](https://deriv.nls.uk/dcn23/9542/95420646.23.pdf), [History of Glasgow, vol. II, ch. XX](https://www.electricscotland.com/history/glasgow/glasgow2_20.htm).
